31.0.0.en: 1- "In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed: deliver me in thy righteousness."

31.0.1.en: 1- It appears from the words of this verse that David was exposed to troubles from his enemies beyond his capacity, but he believed in God and trusted in Him, so his heart was at peace and he was no longer troubled, despite the continued opposition of the enemies.

31.0.2.en: 2- David's perfect faith in God appears in his confidence that God is able to support him all his life, until He transfers him from this life to the better life, that is, eternity.

31.0.3.en: 3- David may have been exposed to a sin and repented of it, so God forgave him, and David trusted in Him to protect him from falling again; indeed, in confidence he feels that God is able to raise him always in a constant relation of love with Him.

31.0.4.en: 4- Because of the harshness of the opposition of the enemies who wrong him, he asked God to deliver him in righteousness, for God is not pleased with injustice, and He supports His weak children.

31.1.0.en: 2- "Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me."

31.1.1.en: 1- David's humility appears in his saying "bow down thine ear to me"; he feels his weakness before the loftiness of God, and asks Him to incline His ear to him.

31.1.2.en: 2- Perhaps the tribulation through which David was passing made him speak in a low voice, and this shows how much he suffered from the threats of the wicked against him. And since his voice was low, he asked God to condescend and bow down His ear to hear him.

31.1.3.en: 3- It appears that David was in severe distress and strong threats from the enemies, who almost overtook him, so he asked God with the boldness of sonship to hasten to him, for he trusts in God's fatherhood and tenderness and His concern to help him.

31.1.4.en: 4- Because of the multitude of enemies David needed to hide from them, and he had nothing before him but God in whom to hide as a fortress and refuge, and in this the Lord delivers him from his enemies.

31.1.5.en: 5- It is a prophecy about Christ, the rock of the fortress and likewise the house of refuge, through His redemption of us on the cross. So whoever takes refuge in the cross of Christ is saved from the warfare of the demons.

31.2.0.en: 3- "For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me."

31.2.2.en: 1- David's hope is the name of God, which delivers him, and he trusts in nothing else, for he has no other power to protect him, and he does not depend on his own strength or the strength of his men; rather, his hope of salvation depends on the grace of God, which He pours out on him for the sake of His holy name.

31.2.3.en: 2- David also depends in his conduct and movements on God, who guides him, and when God guides him his enemies cannot overtake him; for God hides him from their eyes and gives him an escape far from them.

31.2.4.en: 3- The Church counsels that in our spiritual warfare we depend on the name of God and repeat it often, whether through the Jesus Prayer or the Absalis in the Midnight Praise, for it rescues us from the snares of the demons.

31.3.0.en: 4- "Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my fortress."

31.3.1.en: 1- God's protection of David does not mean only stopping the wars directed against him, nor does it mean preventing the possibility of his falling, but it means rescuing him if he falls, so that he does not perish. David trusts in God, his fortress, who will deliver him if he falls into the net.

31.3.2.en: 2- It is a confession by David of his weakness and his need of God, when he said, "Pull me out of the net," and the humble person receives all of God's mercies.

31.3.3.en: 3- David was exposed to many attacks from Saul, not only direct assault but also hidden snares, such as the trickery of some who showed friendship to David so as to deliver him into the hand of Saul, even though David had done good to them, as happened at Keilah (1 Sam 23:12); but David's prayers deliver him because God is his fortress, and God knows the unseen, so He rescues him from all evil.

31.4.0.en: 5- "Into thine hand I commit my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth."

31.4.1.en: 1- When David says "Into thine hand I commit my spirit," it means his complete reliance on God and his faith in God, who protects not only his body but his spirit from every sin, and keeps it in Him.

31.4.2.en: 2- When David commits his spirit into the hand of God, it shows the extent of David's spirituality, who cares for the salvation of his soul more than the comfort of his body, so even if he is exposed to hardships and tribulations from Saul or others, his spirit is kept in the hand of God.

31.4.3.en: 3- David's placing his spirit in the hand of God shows his faith and his heart's preoccupation with eternity, in which his spirit enjoys being with God; for if he longs to enjoy fellowship with God while he is on earth, how much more his longings to enjoy permanent being with Him in eternity.

31.4.4.en: 4- David thanks God who rescued him many times from the hand of his enemies, for by logic David should have died, but God redeemed him and rescued him by miracles, so the arrows of the enemy did not reach him but flew in the air, and he remained kept in the hand of God.

31.4.5.en: 5- It is God who redeemed David, and He is his God of truth; this means that David is wronged and innocent, and God knows this; therefore He rescued him from the hand of his enemies.

31.4.6.en: 6- This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ; David saw with the eye of prophecy Christ dying on the cross and committing His spirit into the hand of the Father, to redeem David and to redeem all mankind. And Christ spoke these words on the cross just before He died (Lk 23:46).

31.5.0.en: 6- "I have hated them that regard lying vanities: but I trust in the Lord."

31.5.1.en: 1- David's enemies trusted in their strength, their position and their wealth, and all these are lying vanities, because they are nothing before the power of God, while David trusted in God alone and not in any other power; therefore he was at peace.

31.5.2.en: 2- Although circumstances, in his flight from the face of Saul, made David take refuge by dwelling among the pagans, he refuses and hates their idol worship and their evil way of life, for in his eyes they are lying vanities, and the truth is God alone; therefore he trusted in Him.

31.5.3.en: 3- David not only refused to rely on the powers of the world but also hated them, because his love for God made anything else rejected and hateful to his heart, for God had filled his heart and satisfied it.

31.5.4.en: 4- All the people around David care for and regard lying vanities, worshiping idols, or caring for money, position and military power, like Saul, but David cared for the worship of God, repeating His holy name, and praying at all times, and this helped him to trust in God.

31.6.0.en: 7- "I will be glad and rejoice in thy mercy: for thou hast considered my trouble; thou hast known my soul in adversities;"

31.6.1.en: 1- When David committed his spirit into the hand of God (v. 5), he of course rejected every sin and was purified by repentance; therefore he received God's mercies and God brought him through the tribulation in peace, and even gave him the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, and for this reason he is in great gladness and joy.

31.6.2.en: 2- David shows God's fatherhood and tenderness in His concern for him and His rescuing him from his adversities; for although He allows the trial, it is only for a time so that man may benefit from it, then He lifts it and compensates man with great tenderness.

31.6.3.en: 3- David received and attained the aim of the trial, which is abasement before God, that is, humility and poverty of spirit and prayer with contrition, so the trial turned into a blessing, and then David experienced God's turning to him and looking upon him, for he is the object of God's love.

31.6.4.en: 4- God allows trials, but in a set measure according to man's endurance, and God, who watches man and looks upon him, lifts the trial at the proper time, for He knows man and the extent of his endurance, so He cannot give him anything beyond his strength; God looked upon David's affliction and knew him in his adversities.

31.7.0.en: 8- "And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room."

31.7.1.en: 1- David thanks God that He delivered him from the hand of his enemies, so they could not seize him, or imprison him, or kill him, or harm him with any bodily harm.

31.7.2.en: 2- At the same time he thanks God for widening the way for him to flee from his enemies, so that he could run far from them, throughout his life and in all his wars, and indeed He gave him victory over his enemies.

31.7.3.en: 3- When David fell into the sin of adultery (2 Sam 11:4) or numbered the people (2 Sam 24:1), God gave him an escape from the hand of Satan, that is, He delivered him through repentance, and he returned to his first state, that is, his sonship.

31.7.4.en: God wants your salvation however great your weakness, so if He allows you tribulations do not be troubled by them, but seek Him and be confident that He delivers you from the hands of the demons, and even gives you the joy of beholding Him.

31.8.0.en: 9- "Have mercy upon me, O Lord, for I am in trouble: mine eye is consumed with grief, yea, my soul and my belly."

31.8.3.en: 1- David faced severe tribulations from Saul's pursuit, or other tribulations that pressed upon his soul and body, and even upon his discernment of what was around him, so he cried out to God to have mercy on him and save him from this distress and all its effects.

31.8.4.en: 2- David's prayer to God means his severe suffering in body and spirit, and that he has no refuge but God, and this confirms two things:

31.8.5.en: a - His humility and showing his need of God.

31.8.7.en: 3- These words of David apply to the Church, which asks God's mercy because of the persecution and tribulations she passes through, so her eyes are spoiled; that is, many of her priests and servants, who are eyes for her, were martyred and tortured. The soul signifies all the spiritual saints, members of the Church, and the body signifies all the people. And when the eye or the soul is spoiled it affects the body; therefore the Church asks God's mercies.

31.9.0.en: 10- "For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of my misery, and my bones are consumed."

31.9.1.en: 1- David expresses the effects of the tribulations upon him, or of his falling into sin, and these effects are:

31.9.5.en: 2- If problems and tribulations continue, the body and soul grow weary, and so David expresses his pains and takes refuge in God, that He may have mercy on him and lift his burdens from him; for he suffered hardships for many long years, which were the period of Saul's pursuit of him.

31.9.6.en: 3- David's taking refuge in God by prayer and sighing is a humility on David's part that makes him receive God's many mercies.

31.10.0.en: 11- "I was a reproach among all mine enemies, and especially among my neighbours, and a fear to mine acquaintance: they that did see me without fled from me."

31.10.1.en: 1- When David fled from the face of Saul, those who knew him thought that he had sinned, and therefore Saul was angry with him, and he deserved death, so David became in their sight an example of shame, and they kept away from him.

31.10.2.en: 2- When David's enemies learned of his flight from the face of Saul they rejoiced over him, and were sure that he was wicked and deserved punishment; indeed, perhaps they helped Saul to arrest him.

31.10.3.en: 3- When David's neighbors and acquaintances learned of his flight from the face of Saul they feared for themselves, so they kept away from him and did not try to help him, lest Saul harm them.

31.10.4.en: 4- These words of David apply to Christ, when the Jews seized Him and tortured Him, then crucified Him, and they apply also to our fathers the martyrs and everyone who endured severe persecutions.

31.11.0.en: 12- "I am forgotten as a dead man out of mind: I am like a broken vessel."

31.11.1.en: 1- It was very painful to David's soul to feel that his neighbors, acquaintances and loved ones, when they found him fleeing from Saul, did not move, and in time considered him lost and dead, so they forgot him and no longer felt for him. This extreme neglect was painful to his soul.

31.11.2.en: 2- When David fled, his acquaintances considered him a broken vessel, that is, refuse and a worthless thing that has been thrown away and got rid of, so David had nothing before him but God, who feels for him and supports him and comforts him.

31.11.3.en: 3- This verse too is a prophecy about Christ, whom they considered like a dead man, despised at His crucifixion and burial, and the world did not know that He is its Savior who died for it.

31.12.0.en: 13- "For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life."

31.12.1.en: 1- David's pains were not limited to his flight from Saul, who wanted to kill him, but he was also exposed to evil words and insults from others, who rejoiced over him and seized the opportunity of his flight to invent from their wicked hearts evil words against him, and he bore them for God's sake.

31.12.2.en: 2- David's enemies cooperated with Saul to destroy him, and devised plots to seize him, but God delivered him from their hands for the sake of his righteousness, and because of their false accusations against him.

31.12.3.en: 3- The threats of Saul and all David's enemies put those who accompanied David in fear; that is, fear came to be on every side around him, but he remained steadfast in his faith.

31.12.4.en: If tribulations come upon you one after another, stand firm in your faith, and lift up your heart in prayer, and be confident that God will not leave you and will surely turn the tribulations into blessings in your life, and bring you out after this into rest.

31.13.0.en: 14- "But I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God."

31.13.1.en: 1- Before the tribulations that met David he found nothing before him but God in whom to trust and to feel peace in His hands.

31.13.2.en: 2- David felt a boldness and a special relationship with God, so he said to Him "my God," and raised prayers to Him in which he poured out his soul before Him, and was at peace in His care and protection of him.

31.14.0.en: 15- "My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me."

31.14.1.en: My times: plural of term, which is the end.

31.14.2.en: 1- The terms are the ends, and David was exposed to death many times, and God rescued him and gave him a new lifespan, so he is assured that all the ends of his life are in the hand of God, and for this reason he devotes himself to prayer and to enjoying fellowship with God who protects him.

31.14.3.en: 2- The terms are also the stages through which David passes in his life, some of which were heavy, like Saul's pursuit of him, and some lighter in troubles, like his reigning over the tribe of Judah and his wars for seven years with Ishbosheth the son of Saul, and some more restful when he reigned over all the children of Israel. In all these David feels that he is in the hand of God, so he lives in His fear, enjoying His love.

31.14.4.en: 3- Since David is at peace in the hand of God, he asks Him in confidence to deliver him from the hand of Saul who pursues him, and from the hand of all his enemies, because God is stronger than all and able to protect him.

31.15.0.en: 16- "Make thy face to shine upon thy servant: save me for thy mercy's sake."

31.15.1.en: 1- David's heart is occupied with God; he wants to enjoy being with Him, and he is not troubled by the enemies because he is assured of God's protection. This shows the extent of David's attachment to the love of God.

31.15.2.en: 2- The shining of God upon David and all mankind was fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ, so David by the spirit of prophecy awaits the appearance of the expected Messiah, the Savior of the whole world, to enlighten the hearts of those who believe in Him.

31.15.3.en: 3- In humility David says to God, I am Your servant, and save me by Your mercy; for David feels his unworthiness in everything, and at the same time he trusts in the mercy of God, which is able to save him from all who trouble him.

31.16.0.en: 17- "Let me not be ashamed, O Lord; for I have called upon thee: let the wicked be ashamed, and let them be silent in the grave."

31.16.1.en: 1- Since David raised his voice in prayer and enjoyed the shining of God, his heart rejoiced and he lived enjoying fellowship with Him; therefore he is confident of victory over his enemies on earth, then of the glory that awaits him in eternal life.

31.16.2.en: 2- Prayer is being with God, and in it man tastes the foretaste of the Kingdom, that is, he feels the sweetness of fellowship with God, and after this it extends into unceasing prayer, which is eternal life. So whoever loves fellowship with God, God lifts him to permanent fellowship with Him in heaven.

31.16.3.en: 3- The wicked who refused to be with God and preferred to be with sin await nothing but shame in hell, to receive the punishment of their sins, and there they feel deprivation of God forever, and this in itself is severe torment.

31.16.4.en: 4- In hell the wicked are silent out of their fear and their shame, for they have nothing with which to justify their sins which they committed on earth, and they know for certain that they deserve this torment; therefore they are silent. And if they had a chance to speak with God on earth, they have lost it in hell, so they are silent and deprived of God forever.

31.17.0.en: 18- "Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous."

31.17.1.en: Put to silence: be made silent, for the dumb is the mute.

31.17.2.en: 1- David asks God, and wishes, that the tongues of the wicked be silenced, which ascribe evil to the righteous, lest they cause them to stumble and weary them.

31.17.3.en: 2- In hell too the wicked lose the ability to speak the vain words that they spoke against the righteous, for they lied and accused them falsely, so the wicked feel their sin, but in despair, and they are silent in the torment.

31.17.4.en: 3- If the righteous man has endured lies, contempt, insolence and pride from the wicked, he is comforted by the joys of heaven, which compensate him for all that he endured, but the wicked are tormented because of all these wrongs they did. The righteous enjoys the praise of God, and the wicked is silent in shame.

31.17.5.en: If you are enduring insults from others, seek God's help, and know that these troubles are temporary, and indeed, as you endure them willingly, God compensates you for them with great glories in heaven.

31.18.0.en: 19- "Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee; which thou hast wrought for them that trust in thee before the sons of men!"

31.18.2.en: 1- David thanks God for His blessings that He poured out on him, for He gave him consolations and peace in his heart, and even joy during the tribulation, so he was not troubled by Saul's pursuit and threats.

31.18.3.en: 2- God's blessings to His children surpass the mind, so that David could not describe them, and said, "Oh how great is thy goodness." They therefore lift man above the tribulation and make him taste the sweetness of heaven while he is on earth.

31.18.4.en: 3- God's blessings and goodness are given by God only to those who fear Him, and not to all mankind; for although God gives general blessings to all mankind, He gives those who fear Him great spiritual blessings, which are the feeling of Him and the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, and these surpass all material and spiritual blessings.

31.18.5.en: 4- God loved His children who revere Him and fear Him; He loved them before the foundation of the world, and laid up for them from eternity countless blessings. This shows God's unlimited love for His children, which satisfies them, so that they need nothing.

31.18.6.en: 5- Whoever fears God keeps away from every sin, carries out His commandments, trusts in Him, and lives at peace among troubled people, and so he is a light for the world and salt for the earth.

31.19.0.en: 20- "Thou shalt cover them with the covering of thy face from the plots of men: thou shalt hide them in a pavilion from the strife of tongues."

31.19.1.en: 1- God covers those who fear Him and trust in Him, and protects them from the plots of the wicked, and as long as God covers them no one can harm them with anything; it is He who preserved David from all of Saul's plots.

31.19.2.en: 2- God covers His children with the covering of His face, so that during the tribulation they see nothing but the face of God, and enjoy His love and fellowship, as happened with the three young men, who praised God and did not feel the fire.

31.19.3.en: 3- When God covers His children with His face and looks upon the plots of men, He spoils them and destroys them, so that they become worthless and do not harm His children, as He spoiled the plot of the wicked against Daniel, so the lions became tame animals and did not harm Daniel.

31.19.4.en: 4- When God covers His children, He gives them wisdom and power in speech, so the wicked cannot overcome them, and all their adversaries become weak before them, as He promised in the New Testament to give His children a mouth and wisdom which all their adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Lk 21:15).

31.19.5.en: 5- God in His love hides His children from evil and the plots devised against them in the pavilion of His care, which signifies the Church in the New Testament. Either He gives them wisdom in their speech with the wicked, or the wicked are not able to prove their words, or He keeps them away from His children in some way, so the children of God always feel God's care and His protection of them.

31.20.0.en: 21- "Blessed be the Lord: for he hath shewed me his marvellous kindness in a strong city."

31.20.1.en: 1- God's love for David the righteous appeared in His protection of him, as if he were in a fortified city, whose high walls cannot be stormed, and these are faith; and this city signifies the Church in the New Testament, surrounded by the angels and saints, and relying on Christ the Head of the Church, who feeds His children with His Body and Blood. It also signifies the perfectly fortified city in heaven, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, where the children of God enjoy fellowship with Him without any disturbance from the demons.

31.20.2.en: 2- David thanks God and blesses Him because He worked miracles in protecting him from Saul's pursuits; for God's mercy made a wonder surpassing the mind, and even delivered Saul into David's hands twice, but David forgave him, so Saul felt shame and confessed it before David, and said to him, "Thou art more righteous than I" (1 Sam 24:17).

31.21.0.en: 22- "For I said in my bewilderment, I am cut off from before thine eyes: nevertheless thou heardest the voice of my supplications when I cried unto thee."

31.21.1.en: 1- When Saul's pursuits of David increased, Satan fought him by casting doubt on God's protection of him, and he was preoccupied with Saul's plots, so he was bewildered and said to himself, has God forgotten me and no longer looks upon me?! So he was in spiritual and psychological distress.

31.21.2.en: 2- But David did not continue in his bewilderment; rather, he returned to what he was accustomed to, which is prayer, and cried out to God, so he regained his peace, and felt God who is with him and protects him, and hears his prayer and supplications.

31.22.0.en: 23- "O love the Lord, all ye his saints: for the Lord preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer."

31.22.1.en: 1- David concludes the psalm with a call to the pious who fear God, that they may enjoy His love, for as they contemplate His love for them, their hearts are drawn to Him and they cling to Him.

31.22.2.en: 2- God cares very much for the faithfulness of His children toward Him, so He blesses them and gives them peace, especially when they hold fast to faithfulness in keeping His commandments, however much tribulations surround them, and in the end He blesses them with many blessings, as happened with David, and made him a great king over all the children of Israel, and subdued his enemies to him, and as He kept faithful Joseph in the house of Potiphar and in the prison, then raised him to the throne of Egypt.

31.22.3.en: 3- On the other hand, the proud wicked, who resist God and wrong His children, God punishes severely, as happened with Saul and his sons, who died in the war with the Philistines (1 Sam 31).

31.23.0.en: 24- "Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that wait for the Lord."

31.23.1.en: 1- In the end David calls those who believe in God to be strong, that is, to stand firm in the faith and not fear the wicked, and likewise to take courage, so that they can attack their enemies with power, because victory is guaranteed to them by the power of God.

31.23.2.en: 2- David calls the believers and styles them those who wait for the Lord, that is, those who are patient in tribulations and bear the pains of striving, for these enjoy God's work in them, which establishes them and encourages them, and as they feel God's support for them, they rejoice in His presence.

31.23.3.en: If tribulations surround you and Satan casts his doubts at you, do not be troubled, but hasten in humility to God, and seek Him and cry out to Him, for He is near to you, and hastens to your aid, and reassures you, and saves you from your enemies.

31.23.4.en: God's blessings for the penitent. Of David. A poem: "Blessed is he whose iniquity is forgiven" (v. 1). Introduction:

31.23.5.en: 1- Its author is David the prophet.

31.23.7.en: After the fifty-first psalm, which begins with the words, "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness." David wrote these two psalms about a year after his fall into adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, when Nathan the prophet came to him and warned him, so he wrote the fifty-first psalm, then wrote this psalm.

31.23.8.en: 3- This psalm is an encouragement to the penitent; if the fifty-first psalm is full of contrition before God, this psalm shows God's blessings to everyone who repents.

31.23.9.en: 4- This psalm is one of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Pss 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).

31.23.10.en: 5- This psalm is also considered, as we mentioned, among the psalms of thanksgiving, which are the psalms (Pss 30-34); here David thanks God who forgives sins.

31.23.11.en: 6- A part of this psalm is mentioned in the sacrament of Baptism, because in it the forgiveness of the sins of the baptized is accomplished.

31.23.12.en: 7- This psalm is considered one of the Pauline psalms, that is, those whose words and thoughts resemble the words and style of St. Paul the Apostle, and they are (Pss 32, 130, 143).

31.23.13.en: 8- St. Augustine loved this psalm and was careful to repeat it until the end of his life.

31.23.14.en: 9- This psalm is called in Hebrew "Asher," which is one of the tribes of the children of Israel and means "happy," because this psalm begins in its first two verses with the word "Blessed," that is, "happy."

31.23.15.en: 10- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
